name: Cold water rinse

lead: A cold water rinse means finishing your hair wash with cool or cold water. The payoff people are after is shinier, smoother-looking hair with no product and no cost.

The idea is that cold water makes the outer cuticle scales lie flatter, so the hair reflects more light and feels smoother. This is the explanation proponents give; no published study has tested cold rinses on hair shine.

paras: People simply turn the water cooler for the last stretch of the shower, after shampoo and conditioner have been rinsed out. It slots into any existing wash routine and is used on every wash or occasionally. Any change in shine would show up right after drying.
No harms specific to the practice have been documented. The main drawback is that cold water on the head and body is uncomfortable for some people.

chain: Cold water at end of wash
angle.text: A final cold rinse is used to make hair look shinier and feel smoother. The belief is that cold water flattens the cuticle so it reflects more light. It is a popular hair-care habit, and no published test of the shine effect exists.

lead: A cold water rinse is a hair-care habit of finishing a wash with cool or cold water. People use it to make hair look shinier and smoother, with the reasoning that cold water closes or flattens the hair cuticle, the outer layer of overlapping scales, so light reflects more evenly and moisture stays in.[1][2]

Stylists and dermatologists quoted in lifestyle coverage describe the technique in these terms. Hairstylist Katelyn Ellsworth says a cold rinse 'seals the cuticle', and New York dermatologist Jody Alpert Levine describes lukewarm water opening the cuticles and a cold rinse closing them.[1] A hair-industry explainer says hot water can lift the cuticle and lead to dryness and frizz, and recommends warm water for washing and a cool finish.[2]

Wikipedia's articles on hair care and hair conditioner describe the cuticle and the roles of shampoo pH and conditioning agents in smoothing it, but do not discuss water temperature.[3][4] No published laboratory or human study of cold water rinses on hair shine was found.
infobox: Warm wash, conditioner, cool final rinse[2]

paras: The practice consists of ending a shower or wash with a final rinse of cold or cool water instead of warm water. It requires no product. The usual routine described by stylists is to wash with warm water and switch to cold at the end.[1][2]

Proponents describe the cold finish as sealing the cuticle so light reflects more evenly and conditioner stays on the hair.[1][2] Wikipedia notes the cuticle is the outer layer of the hair shaft and that damage to the visible shaft cannot be repaired by a biological process.[3]

Wikipedia's conditioner article explains that cationic surfactants press cuticle scales flatter and that acidifiers lower the fibre's negative charge, tighten the cuticle and reduce frizz. Hair's isoelectric point is about pH 3.7.[4] Shampoos in the pH 4 to 6 range are described as the most common because they do not swell the hair shaft.[3] These sources deal with product chemistry and do not test water temperature.
Dermatologist Levine also notes that washing in cold water alone may not remove grime trapped in the cuticles, which is why the cold step is placed at the end.[1]
The rinse is a zero-cost step in hair-care routines aimed at healthier-looking hair. Some people extend it to cold showers generally.
No studies found. No human or laboratory studies of cold water rinses on hair shine, smoothness or cuticle position were located.
